Title Reps and Lenders: A Joint Marketing Plan Agents Will Actually Share

Nov 24, 2026The SocialDM Insights Team9 min read
Key takeaways
  • Agents post content that makes them look helpful and local: verifiable market notes, short explainers, closing day moments and first time buyer guides.
  • RESPA Section 8 limits giving agents things of value for referrals; split joint ads by each party's fair share and clear everything with compliance counsel first.
  • Keep rates and payment examples out of shared posts; Regulation Z disclosure rules apply to any mortgage ad.
  • Start December 1, 2026, send one finished piece a week through February 26, 2027, then keep the two formats agents share most.

Much of what title reps and loan officers send agents never gets posted. Not because agents are lazy, but because the piece is about you, needs editing, or makes the agent wonder if their broker will approve it. The fix is simple to say and harder to do: make content the agent would be proud to post under their own name, make it take ten seconds to share, and run it inside the rules that govern your industry.

This is for title reps, escrow officers and loan officers who market to agents: what agents post, a 90 day plan from December 1, 2026 to February 26, 2027, packaging, measurement and the compliance lines you should not cross.

Why does so much partner content go unposted?

Because it serves the sender, not the agent. Agents protect their feed. A post that looks like an ad for a title company or a rate sheet makes them look like a billboard, so they skip it.

The pieces that get shared share three traits:

  • The agent looks smart. It answers a question their clients already ask.
  • It is local and checkable. The agent can verify every number in under a minute.
  • It is finished. Right size, caption written, nothing to fix.

What will agents actually post?

Five formats, each tied to a real client question. Rotate them so agents never get the same thing twice in a row.

FormatWhat it isWhy an agent shares it
Local market noteThree numbers for one area this month, each with its source namedPast clients and sellers ask "how is the market?" every week
Short explainer videoUnder 60 seconds on one step: what title insurance covers, what a wire fraud warning looks like, what happens at signingSaves the agent from explaining it again
Closing day momentA clean "keys in hand" photo or clip, taken only with the buyer's written permissionCelebrates the agent's client and their work
First time buyer explainerA carousel that walks through one topic, such as earnest money or what an escrow account holdsAgents want to be the patient guide for first time buyers
Q1 planning piece"Thinking about buying or selling in spring 2027? Here is the timeline"Starts conversations in the slow weeks of January

First time buyer explainers have a clear audience. NAR reports that first time buyers fell to a record low of 21% of buyers, with a median age of 40, in its 2025 Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers (transactions from July 2024 through June 2025). Plain, patient explainers suit that buyer.

How to keep a local market note verifiable

Use numbers the agent can check: your title plant's recorded sales counts, the local MLS report, or the county recorder. Name the source and the month on the graphic. Never round in a way that changes the meaning.

What does RESPA allow, and where is the line?

This is the part to get right first. What follows is general information, not legal advice. Before you launch any joint marketing with agents, review it with your compliance team or counsel, and expect the agent to run it past their broker.

Section 8 of RESPA and Regulation X bar giving or accepting any fee, kickback or "thing of value" under an agreement to refer settlement service business. The CFPB's own RESPA FAQs say "thing of value" is broadly defined and that "there is no exception to RESPA Section 8 solely based on the value of the gift or promotion."

Three practical lines follow from that:

  1. Free content can still be a thing of value. Regulation X allows "normal promotional and educational activities" only when they are not conditioned on referrals and do not defray expenses the referral source would otherwise pay. A professionally designed post the agent would otherwise pay a designer for may cross that line. Ask counsel how your materials are treated.
  2. Joint ads should be split by fair share. When both names appear, each party should pay its own share of the cost. An attorney quoted by NAR in 2018 said joint advertising is allowed as long as each party pays its pro rata share, and that online campaigns need a sensible metric for that split. Document how you calculated it.
  3. Marketing services agreements get scrutiny. The CFPB rescinded its 2015 compliance bulletin on MSAs in October 2020 and published new FAQs at the same time, but said the rescission "does not mean that MSAs are per se or presumptively legal." Its FAQs say payments must be reasonably related to the value of services actually performed, and the value of any referrals cannot count.

If you pay for leads or placement on websites or apps, also read the CFPB's February 2023 advisory opinion on digital mortgage comparison shopping platforms, which explains when a platform operator receives a prohibited referral fee. The CFPB withdrew dozens of guidance documents in May 2025, and one law firm's tracker lists this opinion as still active. Guidance keeps shifting, so confirm the current status with counsel.

What rules apply to lender content?

A post that promotes loan terms can count as a mortgage ad. Under Regulation Z, an advertised rate must be stated as an "annual percentage rate," using that term. If a post names a down payment amount or percentage, a number of payments, a payment amount or a finance charge, it triggers more disclosures, including the down payment, the repayment terms and the APR.

The safe pattern for shared content: no rates, no payment examples, no "as little as" lines in anything the agent posts. Keep those in your own compliance reviewed ads, and have your compliance team or counsel review any lender content before it goes out.

Fair lending and fair housing apply too. FDIC supervised banks that advertise home loans must prominently indicate they lend without regard to protected classes, for example with the Equal Housing Lender logo, and other lenders have their own regulator's rules. For the agent side, HUD says the Fair Housing Act prohibits discriminatory real estate advertising, including ads placed on websites. Describe homes, places and processes, never the kind of people who belong somewhere.

What does the 90 day plan look like?

Three phases, one theme each. Send one ready piece per week, every Tuesday, so agents learn when to expect it.

Phase 1: Set up and year end moments (December 1 to December 31, 2026)

  • Week of December 1: Get your compliance sign off on the format list, cost split method and disclaimers. Pick 10 to 15 agents you already work with.
  • Week of December 7: Call each agent. Ask three questions: what do clients ask you most, what did you post this year that worked, and what would you never post?
  • Week of December 14: First piece: a closing day explainer, "What to bring to closing," plus the holiday closing schedule for your office.
  • Week of December 21: A year end closing day moment template the agent fills with their own client photo, with permission.

Phase 2: Q1 planning and first time buyers (January 4 to January 31, 2027)

  • Week of January 4: Q1 planning carousel: "Buying in spring 2027? Here is your 12 week timeline."
  • Week of January 11: First local market note, December numbers, sources named.
  • Week of January 18: First time buyer explainer: what earnest money is and where it goes.
  • Week of January 25: Short video: "What title insurance protects," under 60 seconds, captioned.

Phase 3: Repeat what worked (February 1 to February 26, 2027)

  • Week of February 1: January market note.
  • Week of February 8: Second first time buyer explainer, picked from questions agents sent you.
  • Week of February 15: Wire fraud warning video, worth sending to every agent.
  • Week of February 22: Review the numbers below with each agent. Decide what runs in March.

For agents who want more, point them to what to film each week and the broader 2027 marketing plan for agents.

How do you make it easy to share?

Remove every step between "nice" and "posted."

  • Send it where they work. A text with the files attached beats a portal login.
  • Two sizes, always. A square or 4:5 post and a vertical 9:16 story or reel version.
  • Two captions. One plain, one warmer. Under 100 words each. The agent picks their voice.
  • Agent first branding. Their name and brokerage most visible, as their broker and state rules require. Yours smaller, only as your compliance team approves.
  • A one line "why." "Post this Tuesday or Wednesday; it answers the question buyers ask before an offer."
  • No rates, no claims to check. If it needs a disclosure, it is not a share piece.

A text script you can send

"Hi Jordan, this week's piece is a 45 second video on what to bring to closing. Two sizes and two captions are attached. Everything in it is general, no rates. Want me to swap in a photo from one of your closings next time?"

How do you measure it?

Keep one sheet with a row per agent per piece.

MeasureHow to get itWhat it tells you
Share ratePieces posted divided by pieces sent, by agent and by formatWhich formats agents trust
Saves and shares on the agent's postAsk the agent for a screenshot of insights after 7 daysWhether their audience found it useful
Replies and messagesAsk the agent if any client mentioned itWhether it started conversations
RequestsCount agents who ask for a topic or a custom versionReal demand for the program

Do not track or report agent referrals as a measure of this program. Tying marketing to referral counts is exactly the pattern RESPA scrutinizes. Measure usefulness and reach.

By February 26, 2027, make the two formats agents post most the backbone of your March to May plan.

Where does AI search fit?

Clients may look an agent up in Google and AI tools before they call. Consistent, local, plain explainers posted under the agent's name give those tools something specific to find. We cover that side in how agents get recommended by ChatGPT and Google AI.

Questions we hear

What are good title rep marketing ideas for 2027?

Content agents can post under their own name: local market notes with named sources, short explainer videos, closing day moments shared with client permission, first time buyer explainers and Q1 planning timelines. Send one finished piece a week on the same day.

Is co marketing between lenders, title reps and agents allowed under RESPA?

It can be, but RESPA Section 8 bars giving a thing of value for referrals, and the CFPB says there is no exception based only on the value of a gift or promotion. Joint ads should be paid by each party according to its pro rata share of the cost. This is not legal advice; check with your compliance counsel.

Can a loan officer put a rate in a post an agent shares?

It is best not to. Under Regulation Z an advertised rate must be stated as an annual percentage rate, and terms like a payment amount or down payment trigger more disclosures. Keep rates in your own compliance reviewed ads, and have counsel or your compliance team review lender content.

How often should I send agents content?

Once a week on a fixed day is easy for agents to expect and for you to keep up. Review what got posted after about 90 days.

How do I know if a joint marketing program is working?

Track share rate by format, saves and shares on the agent's posts, client replies and how many agents ask for more. Do not measure the program by referral counts.
